chunks: "The big advantages of a LiPo are shape, weight and energy density.
Because it's a pouch with no rigid can, you can make it thin and any shape, it's lighter, and it has high energy per kilogram, roughly two to three times NiMH and many times lead-acid.
Good LiPo cells also have low internal resistance, so they can deliver high current, which is why drones and RC use them. The trade-offs: first, mechanical.
The pouch is soft and fragile; a puncture, bend or sharp edge is dangerous, so the product has to protect it.
Second, swelling: as it ages or if it's abused, it generates gas and bulges, and there's no can to contain that, so you need room in the enclosure.
Third, like any lithium-ion cell it needs a protection circuit and a proper charger, because overcharge, over-discharge or a short can lead to fire.
Fourth, aging and temperature: heat and high state of charge shorten life, and you can't charge it cold.
Fifth, cost: cylindrical cells are made in huge volume, so per kilowatt-hour they're often cheaper, and a custom-shaped LiPo needs tooling.
Versus other batteries, it loses on cost and robustness to lead-acid and NiMH, loses on cycle life and safety to LiFePO4, and loses on shelf life to primary lithium cells.
It's the best choice when size, weight and energy density matter most."
